earlyIntervention.title: Why Early Intervention Matters
earlyIntervention.excerpt: The first years of a child's life offer a critical window for developmental support — here's why acting early makes such a measurable difference.

body.h1: A critical window for the developing brain
body.p1: Research consistently shows that a child's brain is most adaptable in the first few years of life. Starting therapy during this window — rather than waiting for a child to "grow out of it" — gives interventions far more room to reshape developmental trajectories.
body.caption1: A parent and child building early language skills together at home.
body.p2: Early intervention isn't just about therapy sessions at a center. It's about equipping families with strategies they can use every day, turning ordinary moments — mealtime, bath time, play — into opportunities for growth.
body.quote1: The earlier we start, the more a child's daily environment becomes part of the treatment plan, not separate from it.
body.p3: If you've noticed a developmental delay, however small, the most helpful next step is a professional assessment — not waiting to see if it resolves on its own.

speechMilestones.title: Speech & Language Milestones: What to Expect
speechMilestones.excerpt: A practical guide to the language milestones most children reach by certain ages, and when it's worth asking a specialist for guidance.

body.h1: What typical language development looks like
body.p1: By 12 months, most children say their first words. By 2 years, simple two-word phrases. By 3, short sentences. These are general guideposts, not strict deadlines — every child develops at their own pace.
body.p2: What matters more than hitting an exact age is the overall trend: is a child's communication steadily expanding, or has it plateaued for several months?
body.caption1: A specialist working through communication exercises during a session.
body.p3: If a child isn't combining words by age 2, or their speech is difficult for family members to understand by age 3, a speech and language evaluation can identify exactly where extra support would help most.

sensoryPlay.title: The Power of Sensory Play at Home
sensoryPlay.excerpt: Simple, low-cost sensory activities parents can set up at home to support a child's developmental progress between therapy sessions.

body.h1: Why sensory input matters for development
body.p1: Sensory play — activities involving touch, movement, sound, and texture — helps children build the neural pathways behind attention, self-regulation, and fine motor skills.
body.caption1: Sorting colorful wooden blocks together builds focus and fine motor coordination.
body.p2: You don't need special equipment: sorting blocks by color, digging through a bin of rice or beans, or simply stacking cups all count as meaningful sensory practice.
body.quote1: The best sensory activities are the ones a child wants to repeat — repetition is where the real learning happens.

familyReading.title: Building Language Through Everyday Reading
familyReading.excerpt: Reading together isn't just a bedtime routine — it's one of the most effective, evidence-backed ways to build a child's vocabulary and communication skills.

body.p1: Shared reading exposes children to far more vocabulary than everyday conversation alone, and the back-and-forth of pointing, naming, and asking questions builds early communication skills long before a child can read themselves.
body.p2: It doesn't need to be a long book or a quiet moment — reading in short bursts, anywhere, still counts. What matters is consistency and genuine engagement, not perfect conditions.
body.caption1: A few minutes of shared reading, wherever you are, adds up over time.
body.p3: Try narrating what's happening on the page, pausing to let your child predict what comes next, and following their interest even if it means skipping pages.
